newsitem.title: CUBA: Cubans generally welcome prospect of Papal visit.
newsitem.headline: Cubans generally welcome prospect of Papal visit.

text.p: Cubans, whether supporters of the government or Roman Catholics, generally welcomed news on Tuesday that President Fidel Castro had met Pope John Paul and that the pontiff will come to the island next year.
Castro himself described his meeting at the Vatican as a "miracle".

"We are waiting anxiously for this visit by the pope," said Maria de Lourdes Cuervo, a Roman Catholic who works as a volunteer distributing donated medicines and clothes at Santa Rita church in Havana's Miramar district.
"This meeting (between Castro and the pope) is very important," Cuervo told Reuters, adding it showed how much relations between the Cuban authorities and the church had eased recently.

Castro, one of the world's last surviving communist leaders, met the pope for the first time at the Vatican earlier on Tuesday. The pontiff accepted Castro's invitation to travel to the Caribbean island, the only Spanish-speaking country in Latin America he has not visited, next year.
State television reported the meeting as the first item on its noon news bulletin, showing the Cuban leader shaking hands with the pontiff and receiving a bible from him.
Speaking later in remarks broadcast by Cuban television, Castro was full of praise for the pope and said it was a "miracle" he had been able to greet him.

Gloria Guerra, a teacher praying at the church of Santa Rita, told Reuters the prospect of a papal visit was "very lovely". "We (Cuban Catholics) never thought we would be able to see him," added Guerra.

Communist Party member Orestes Calderon, riding through Miramar on a bicycle, said that while he was not a Catholic, he welcomed the prospect of the papal visit because the pontiff was a figure of world importance.

But the retired aviation engineer blamed the church for often tense church-state relations since the 1959 revolution. He said that in the past the church had catered to well-off white people rather than humble black people like himself.

Before the revolution, he said, there was a Catholic school in his neighbourhood. "How many black pupils were there? Just one," Calderon said, adding that among all Havana's priests at the time there was just one who was black.

It was not just the official concept of the church being at odds with Marxist ideology and alien to ordinary working Cubans that strained relations. Cuba's Catholic bishops have also periodically urged political change on the island.
In recent years plainclothes security agents often policed church services marking important religious festivals.

But official apprehension over the role of the church appears to have eased recently. Cuban authorities have also welcomed the Vatican's condemnation of Washington's 34-year-old economic embargo on Cuba.
